```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`rho_GE` is the correlation, across genes, of the effect that genetically regulated expression has
on two traits. It is estimated in four steps: instruments, a joint model per gene, aggregation
across tissues, and the correlation itself.

The package ships 25 chromosome-22 genes with their real skeletal-muscle instruments and two small
simulated GWAS, so every step below runs here.

```{r setup}
library(rhoGE)
set.seed(1)   # FusioMR is a sampler
x <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "rhoGE")
```

## Instruments

Instruments are cis-eQTLs below a P threshold, LD-pruned within a window, keeping genes with at
least five of them. `build_instruments()` does this against a PLINK reference panel; it is the slow
step and depends only on the eQTL resource, so build it once and reuse it for every pair of traits.
A prebuilt GTEx v10 set over 50 tissues is on the release page. Here we load the shipped subset:

```{r}
iv <- data.table::fread(x("instruments_chr22_muscle.tsv.gz"))
head(iv, 3)
```

## Both traits in one model

`read_gwas()` matches the usual column names automatically. `fusio_pair()` aligns each instrument
to both GWAS and fits the single-exposure, multiple-outcome model of FusioMR, which keeps the two
effects on a common scale and shares information about pleiotropy between them.

```{r}
g1 <- read_gwas(x("gwas_trait1.tsv.gz"))
g2 <- read_gwas(x("gwas_trait2.tsv.gz"))
fit <- fusio_pair(g1, g2, iv, control = FusioMR::parameter_control(niter = 4000))
head(fit, 3)
```

## One row per gene

With several tissues, `aggregate_genes()` combines their P values with ACAT and takes the direction
from the most significant tissue. ACAT is valid under arbitrary correlation between tissues, so
adding tissues does not multiply the number of tests.

```{r}
genes <- aggregate_genes(fit)
co <- data.table::fread(x("gene_coords_v19.tsv.gz"), col.names = c("gene", "chr", "pos"))
genes <- merge(genes, co, by = "gene")
```

## The correlation, and the directional classes

Neighbouring genes share instruments, so the confidence interval comes from a jackknife over
genomic blocks rather than over genes.

```{r}
rho_ge(genes, block = genes$pos %/% 5e6, chr = genes$chr, pos = genes$pos)
cls <- direction_classes(genes)
cls$shares
c(antagonistic = cls$antagonistic, n = cls$n_genes, P = cls$P)
```

Each selected gene is returned with its class and with `type`, antagonistic or synergistic, and the
binomial test asks whether the two are equally common. The class names come from the disease–fitness
setting, where an expression change that raises liability while raising fitness is antagonistic;
rename them if that reading does not fit your two traits.
